title: How to remember interview details for many candidates: a Mac system for recruiters
metaTitle: How to remember interview details for many candidates on Mac
description: Recruiters lose interview details fast. Use same-day notes, one note per candidate, Apple Notes search and a tracker to recall every candidate on Mac.
targetKeyword: how to remember interview details for many candidates
secondaryKeywords: recruiter candidate tracker in Google Sheets
intro: To remember interview details for many candidates, write a short note right after each call. Keep one note per candidate in one place you can search. Memory fades fast, and similar screens blur together by the end of the week. The routine below takes a few minutes a day and works on a Mac with Apple Notes, Google Sheets, and the calendar you already use.
tldr: Write a verdict line and two quotes within minutes of each call, while the details are fresh.
Keep one note per candidate, named by role, name and date, in one searchable app.
File scorecards by the next business day. Greenhouse recommends that timeline, and says sooner is better.
Notes help you form a fairer overall view. They do not fix every trait rating on their own.
Lazur can dictate notes at your cursor with fn and point at search controls. You still check the text and file the scorecard.

blocks.text: Recalling details across many interviews is partly a memory problem and partly a paper trail problem. By the middle of a busy week, the first candidate's best answer has faded. You remember the last person you spoke to and the one who made you laugh. A better memory will not fix that. A habit of writing details down while they are fresh will.

Most recruiters do not need a lecture on memory. They need a routine they can repeat on a busy Tuesday. The routine below works with tools you already have on a Mac. It also fits the honest limits of the research, which is thinner than most blog posts suggest.
What the research says about memory and interview notes

Start with the honest answer. No peer-reviewed study measures how fast recruiters forget candidates across a hiring pipeline. Nobody has priced the cost of a mixed-up candidate in dollars. What exists comes from neighboring work, and you should read it with that caveat in mind.

The best-known memory curve comes from Hermann Ebbinghaus. A 2015 replication in PLOS ONE, by Murre and Dros, followed one subject. That person relearned word lists after intervals from 20 minutes to 31 days. The curve matched Ebbinghaus's original data closely. That is one person and word lists, not interviews. It still shows the shape. Loss comes fast, and it keeps going.

Interview notes have their own study. In 1999, Biesanz, Neuberg, Judice and Smith tested simulated interviews. Note-taking reduced the effect of negative expectations on interviewers' overall impressions. It did not reduce bias in ratings of the specific traits those expectations concerned. So notes can make your overall view fairer. They do not fix every score on their own.

blocks.title: Evidence limits
blocks.text: The memory numbers come from a single-subject word-list study. The interview numbers come from simulated interviews. Use them to justify the habit, not to predict your own recall rate.
When to write each part of the note

Split the work by time, not by candidate. During the call, jot quotes, specific examples, and two or three questions you still need answered. Right after the call, write a verdict line and your top concerns. Then file the scorecard in your applicant tracking system before its deadline.

rows: Direct quotes, specific examples, open questions
One note per candidate in Apple Notes
Verdict line, two strengths, two concerns
Same note, verdict at the top
Scorecard with a score for each criterion
Check for missing scorecards and send reminders
blocks.caption: Timing for one interview. Match the deadline to your employer's scorecard rules.

blocks.text: Set up one note per candidate in Apple Notes

Apple Notes already comes with your Mac, so start there. Make a folder for each open role. Press ⌘N or choose File > New Note to start a note. Name it with the role, the candidate's name, and the date. For example: Support lead, Priya N, 9 Nov. The same title format makes every note easy to scan.

Use one template in every note. Put the verdict first, then evidence, then concerns, then the next step. The order matters. A reader who opens the note at a debrief sees the decision before the detail.

items: Verdict: advance, hold, or decline, with one line on why
Evidence: two or three quotes or examples, in the candidate's own words where you can
Concerns: what still needs checking, and who can check it
Next step: the person, the date, and the question to ask

blocks.text: Finding the note later is the hard part. Inside an open note, press ⌘F to search that note. To search every note, click the Search button in the Notes toolbar. Then use the arrow beside the magnifying glass. Choose All Accounts if you use more than one account. Apple's search also reads attachment filenames, PDFs, and scanned documents.

Locked notes show only their titles in search results, so a locked candidate note will not surface by its text. Menu names can also shift between macOS versions. If a button is not where this page says, look for the magnifying glass and work from there.
Run a tracker so each candidate has one row

Notes hold the detail. A sheet holds the status. In Google Sheets, make one row per candidate. Use columns for role, stage, interview date, verdict, scorecard deadline, and a link to the note. Freeze the top row so the headers stay in view. Add a dropdown for stage so the same words appear in every row.

Step-by-step help is on [freezing the top row](/how-to/freeze-the-top-row-in-google-sheets) and [creating a dropdown list](/how-to/create-a-dropdown-list-in-google-sheets). For a starting layout, see [Google Sheets for recruiters](/for/recruiters/google-sheets).

Sort the tracker by scorecard deadline each morning. Anything due today or overdue moves to the top. That one habit shows which feedback is late before anyone asks. For sorting steps, see [sorting data by column](/how-to/sort-data-by-column-in-google-sheets).
A worked example from one busy week

Say you run screens on three days for the same support lead role. Each call is with a different candidate. By Friday, the Monday calls can blur into one conversation. Here is how the system changes that week.

After each call, open the candidate's note and type the verdict and two quotes. A few minutes of typing beats a rebuild from memory on Friday. If you prefer to speak, hold fn and dictate the same content. Then read it back before you save.

On Friday, search the notes for a phrase you remember, such as on-call or Zendesk. The right note opens, and you are not guessing which candidate said it. That search is the payoff for writing the note in the first place.

Thursday's tracker shows one scorecard still missing from Monday. You message that interviewer the same day, and include the deadline in the message. The hiring manager gets a complete set before the decision meeting.
Mistakes that make the problem worse

items: Writing adjectives instead of evidence. 'Good communicator' tells nobody anything. Write what the candidate said or did.
Batching notes at the end of the week. Memory has already smoothed out the details by then.
Keeping notes in chat threads, sticky notes, or a personal notebook. These rarely reach the hiring record.
Treating one verdict as a summary of the whole interview. Notes help with overall impressions, not every trait score.
Recording calls without checking the rules. Consent and retention rules vary by employer and location.
Pasting candidate details into any AI tool before checking your employer's rules on personal data.

blocks.text: Privacy and AI tools for candidate notes

Recruiters handle personal data about applicants. Many employers set rules on where that data can go. Follow your employer's rules on client, candidate, or patient data before you use any AI tool, notetaker, or dictation tool. If your team works under stricter rules, those rules win.

Granola is a Mac meeting-notes app that says it captures audio without a bot in the participant list. Its pricing page lists a Basic plan with 30 days of meeting history. Business is $14 per user per month, and Enterprise is $35 per user per month. Check the pricing page for current terms before you rely on them.

Lazur's privacy terms are simple. It listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those terms do not replace your employer's data rules.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold fn to dictate clean text at your cursor in any app. That helps when you want to say your verdict out loud right after a call. It does not decide the verdict for you, and it does not file scorecards for you.

Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about what is on screen. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where the search control sits in Apple Notes, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to build a dropdown in Google Sheets, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur drafts and types text. Give it your bullet points and ask for a follow-up to the hiring manager. Read the draft, edit it, and send it yourself. Lazur does not click Send for you. For Gmail routines, see [Gmail for recruiters](/for/recruiters/gmail) and [scheduling an email to send later](/how-to/schedule-an-email-to-send-later-in-gmail).
Compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing). Lazur runs on the Mac, and Windows is planned, not available. If your team works on Windows, this is not your tool yet.
Next steps for this week

items: Create one Apple Notes folder for the role you are filling now.
Write the four-heading template in a note called Template, then copy it for each candidate.
Make a Google Sheets tracker with one row per candidate and a deadline column.
Set a calendar reminder for each scorecard deadline, with one business day as the default.
Check your employer's rules on notes, recording, and AI tools before you use them on candidate data.

blocks.text: Start with the verdict line on your next call. The rest of the system grows from that one habit.

faq.question: How do I remember interview details for many candidates without recording calls?
faq.answer: Write a verdict line and two quotes right after each call, in one note per candidate. Recording is not required, and it may be restricted. Check your employer's policy and local consent rules before you record any call.

faq.question: How fast should I write interview notes?
faq.answer: Write them right after the call, while the details are fresh. Greenhouse recommends scorecards within one business day, and says sooner is better. The Ebbinghaus replication shows steep loss over days, though it used word lists, so do not wait for the end of the week.

faq.question: Does taking notes during an interview hurt rapport?
faq.answer: The research is limited. A 1999 simulated-interview study found note-taking changed how expectations shaped overall impressions, but it did not test rapport. Tell candidates you take notes, keep them short, and look up between points. This is practical advice, not a proven fix.

faq.question: Can Lazur take my interview notes for me?
faq.answer: Lazur dictates text at your cursor when you hold fn, and you check the text before you save it. Lazur does not operate other apps for you, so you still file scorecards in your applicant tracking system yourself.

faq.question: Is it safe to put candidate details into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on personal data first. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer you, are not stored, and are never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Which Apple Notes search should I use for old candidates?
faq.answer: Press ⌘F inside an open note to search that note. For all notes, click the Search button, then use the arrow beside the magnifying glass. Choose All Accounts if you have more than one account. Locked notes show only their titles.

faq.question: What if my employer does not provide a scorecard?
faq.answer: Use the four-heading template as your own working record. Keep it where your company allows candidate details to be stored. Ask your recruiting lead which tools are approved before you start.

faq.question: Are the Apple Notes steps the same on every macOS version?
faq.answer: Not verified for every version. Apple's guide did not state which macOS versions its steps cover, and menu names can shift. If a control is not where this page says, look for the magnifying glass and work from there.

costs.title: Admin time that adds up
costs.text: IrishJobs reports recruiters spend an average of 5.96 hours every week on manual and administrative tasks, based on a survey of 250 businesses in Ireland. That survey does not measure recall time, so treat it as context. Each time you rebuild a candidate's story from memory, you add to that admin load.

costs.title: Slower hiring
costs.text: SHRM's 2025 benchmarking reports say screening and interviewing alone average 8 to 9 days each. Late or vague feedback sits inside that window. Notes will not fix the whole timeline, but they stop you waiting on your own memory.

costs.title: Money per hire
costs.text: SHRM puts the average cost per hire at $5,475 for nonexecutive roles and $35,879 for executive roles, from 2,371 member responses. Notes take minutes. A poor hire costs far more, though no study prices recall errors directly.

costs.title: Judgment you cannot explain later
costs.text: Interview notes support the fairness of your decision. In a simulated-interview study, note-taking reduced the effect of expectations on overall impressions. Without notes, you may reach a verdict you cannot defend to a hiring manager or a candidate.

costs.title: Stress on a busy week
costs.text: The same IrishJobs survey reports that 33% of recruiters experience high levels of physical and mental stress. The article does not state the survey year. A pile of half-written notes adds to that load.

causes.title: Memory fades in days
causes.text: In a PLOS ONE replication of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, one subject relearned word lists after intervals from 20 minutes to 31 days. Recall falls fast early on. That study used word lists, not interviews, so read it as a pattern, not a measurement of recruiters.

causes.title: Similar candidates blur together
causes.text: Most screens for one role ask the same questions. Answers sound alike within a day. The details that matter, like a specific project or a tricky stakeholder, get overwritten by the next call.

causes.title: Feedback waits too long
causes.text: Scorecards filed late mean you write from the last interview you remember best. Greenhouse recommends submitting at least one business day after an interview, and says the sooner the better. It sends interviewers a reminder one hour after each interview ends.

causes.title: Expectations shape judgment
causes.text: Biesanz and colleagues found that negative expectations biased interviewers' overall impressions in simulated interviews. Note-taking reduced that effect on overall impressions, but not on ratings of the specific traits involved. Notes help, but they do not cancel bias.

causes.title: Notes live in too many places
causes.text: Sticky notes, direct messages, a paper pad, and a shared doc per role all hold a piece of the story. Each place is a separate search. When you need one detail, you check four apps and may still miss it.

causes.title: No one owns the full record
causes.text: Each interviewer keeps their own notes. The recruiter sees the summary, not the detail. The hiring manager asks for specifics that nobody wrote down, and the recruiter has to guess.

fixes.title: Write a verdict line before the next call
fixes.text: Within minutes of the call, write one line: the candidate, the role, your verdict, and the strongest reason. Then add two quotes or examples. This habit keeps the most useful detail from fading. It only works if you do it before the next call starts.

fixes.title: Use one template for every candidate
fixes.text: Use the same four headings in every note: verdict, evidence, concerns, next step. Matching headings let you scan your notes in the same order and compare candidates side by side later.

fixes.title: Keep one note per candidate in one place
fixes.text: Apple Notes on your Mac works well. Name each note with the role, the name, and the date. Inside an open note, press ⌘F to search it. To search all notes, click the Search button and choose All Accounts if you use more than one account.

fixes.title: Put every scorecard deadline on your calendar
fixes.text: Create a calendar event for each scorecard due date when you schedule the call. Use one business day as your default. Greenhouse recommends that timeline as a minimum target, and says the sooner the better.

fixes.title: Ask the same questions in the same order
fixes.text: A fixed question order gives your notes a structure. Write the question number next to each quote. You can then compare answers across candidates without relying on memory for what each person was asked.

fixes.title: Dictate your notes straight after the call
fixes.text: Hold fn and say your verdict and quotes. Lazur dictates clean text at your cursor in any app. Read it back before you save, since dictation can mishear names, schools, and job titles.

fixes.title: Use a notetaker only where your rules allow it
fixes.text: Granola captures audio without a bot in the participant list, and it can add AI text beside your own notes. Check your employer's policy and local consent rules first. Without approval, skip it and keep handwritten or typed notes.

plan.label: Right after
plan.title: Write the verdict line
plan.text: Before the next call starts, add the verdict and two quotes to the candidate's note. Keep it short. Anything longer can wait until the scorecard is filed.

plan.label: Same day
plan.title: File the scorecard and update the tracker
plan.text: Submit the scorecard in your applicant tracking system. Check that the note and the scorecard say the same thing. Update the tracker row with the verdict and the next step.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Sort by deadline and send reminders
plan.text: Sort the Google Sheets tracker by scorecard deadline. Message each interviewer whose feedback is late, with the due date in the message. Copy the hiring manager only after a deadline has passed.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Skim the week's notes
plan.text: Open each note for the open role. Look for missing verdicts, vague words, and open questions. Close the questions you can settle with a short call or email.

plan.label: Before debrief
plan.title: Bring quotes, not memory
plan.text: Search the notes for the phrases the team will ask about, such as on-call or a specific tool. Bring the quotes to the decision meeting, not your recollection of them.

plan.label: Next role
plan.title: Copy the template and tracker
plan.text: Duplicate the note template and tracker for the new role. Start the routine on the first screen of the new hiring push, not after the tenth.
